title: Tell Robot What Not to Do: A Negation Understanding Perspective

paper.title: Tell Robot What Not to Do: A Negation Understanding Perspective
paper.abstract:
Abstract Instruction following enables robots to perform diverse tasks specified in natural language, making it a fundamental capability for human–robot interaction.
Beyond communicating desired outcomes, users also need to specify constraints on what not to do .
We investigate how to enable vision-language-action models (VLAs) to follow negated instructions, where robots must accomplish task goals while respecting explicit exclusions.
To this end, we propose NegaAlign, a parameter-efficient, plug-and-play framework that extends pretrained VLAs to follow negated instructions through image–language supervision alone.
Specifically, we introduce Negation Transformation Layers into selected layers of the vision–language backbone to reshape intermediate instruction representations.
Meanwhile, teacher-guided alignment mechanism is designed to align the instruction-relevant visual tokens, transferring action-relevant grounding from instructions that satisfy the negated constraint.
Training phase uses supervision constructed from existing demonstrations and updates only the inserted layers, keeping all pretrained parameters frozen, including the action generator.
We further introduce NegaBench, a simulation benchmark spanning 10 scenarios across five domains for systematically evaluating manipulation under negated constraints.
Experiments across GR00T, π 0 \pi_{0} , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} demonstrate consistent improvements in negated instruction following.
With 11.6M trainable parameters, NegaAlign increases the negated-instruction success rate of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} from 2.60% to 88.45% on NegaBench and from 12.4% to 88.8% on real-world tasks, while retaining performance on affirmative instructions.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: Existing VLAs struggle with negated instructions, risking unsafe actions. Our proposed NegaAlign enables actions under negated constraints. As robots enter daily life, reliable instruction following is crucial for both human and robot safety. Vision Language Action models (VLAs) Zitkovich et al. (2023) ; Kim et al. (2025) ; Intelligence et al. (2025) ; Bjorck et al. (2025) follow natural language instructions and perform manipulation tasks in complex environments. Pretraining on large-scale embodied datasets O’Neill et al. (2024) enables them to complete a wide range of manipulation tasks, including pick-and-place, tool use, and object rearrangement. However, these existing VLAs are mostly trained on affirmative instructions and struggle to follow negated instructions. This limitation can result in unsafe or undesired actions Chen et al. (2026b) ; Lyu et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2025) , as the robot may act on the affirmative content of the instruction without considering the negated constraints. For example, given ”Give me a tool, except the knife”, a robot will still hand the knife to the user, which is an extremely dangerous behavior in daily life, as illustrated in Figure 1 (a). A key source of this problem lies in the VLMs backbone, whose difficulty in understanding negation affects the action sequence generation of VLAs further. Existing studies investigate negation understanding in image-text matching Dobreva and Keller (2021) ; Aggarwal et al. (2026) , image editing Bui et al. (2025) , and image-grounded object detection Kang et al. (2026) ; Yang et al. (2026) , which could not be applied to the VLAs directly since the VLAs need to ground the negated instruction into the sequence of actions to complete the task. Recent approaches improve VLA instruction following through hierarchical decomposition and fine-grained supervision Zawalski et al. (2024) ; Zhu et al. (2024) . Hi Robot Shi et al. (2025) uses an additional VLM to decompose instructions into subtasks, introducing extra inference computation. APT Xu et al. (2026) adopts two-stage pretraining to better preserve VLM knowledge in the action expert, but requires a dedicated multi-stage training procedure, while Fine-VLA Hu et al. (2026) constructs fine-grained instruction data to strengthen language-action alignment. However, collecting negation-specific robot demonstrations is costly and time-consuming. Hence, how to enable existing VLAs to follow negated instructions without additional negation-specific embodied data remains an unexplored problem. To address these challenges, we propose NegaAlign, a parameter-efficient, plug-and-play framework for following negated instructions without costly negation-specific embodied data for the reliable instruction following. Our key insight is that when action expert generates the action sequences, most information are provided by the visual tokens, while the vision tokens are grounded by the instruction text representations. Specifically, we firstly construct teacher-student instruction pairs from existing affirmative-task data and hand-crafted negated instructions without additional negation-specific action data. Subsequently, we propose sophisticated Negation Transformation Layers into selected layers of the VLM backbone to revise intermediate instruction representations of negated instructions, which help to modulate the instruction representations to be more compatible with the negated constraints. Meanwhile, we apply teacher-guided alignment to instruction-relevant visual tokens. The alignment propagates the revised instruction representations to the visual tokens which is beneficial for the action generation. Training phase updates only the inserted layers using image–language supervision, while the pretrained backbone and action expert remain frozen. To evaluate the capability of reliable instruction following, we establish NegaBench, a simulation benchmark spanning 10 scenarios across five domains for systematically evaluating manipulation under negated constraints. Experiments on the NegaBench and real-world robot demonstrate that NegaAlign significantly improves the success rate of negated instruction following across various scenarios with fewer update of parameters. The main contributions of this work are listed as follows: • We present the first investigation of negated instruction understanding and execution in VLAs, revealing how semantics from language instructions are encoded in internal representations and gradually propagate through the model to shape action generation. • We propose NegaAlign, a plug-and-play framework which revises instruction representations through Negation Transformation Layers and propagates negation semantics to visual representations through Teacher-Guided Visual Alignment, enabling VLAs to follow negated constraints efficiently by updating only a few number of parameters. • We establish NegaBench, a benchmark for systematically evaluating robotic manipulation under negated instructions. Experiments in simulation and real-world robot demonstrate that NegaAlign substantially improves negated instruction following across multiple existing VLAs while preserving performance on affirmative instructions.

sections.heading: 2.1 Negation in Language, Vision, and Action
sections.text: Negation remains challenging for large language models (LLMs) despite their strong general capabilities. Evaluations show that LLMs degrade on negated prompts, sometimes worsening with scale, and struggle with negated commonsense knowledge Jang et al. (2023) ; Wang et al. (2026) . Mechanistic analyses further reveal that shortcut behaviors can disrupt how LLMs suppress or reconstruct negated meanings Zhou et al. (2026) . Similar challenges arise in vision-language models (VLMs), where negated semantics must be grounded in visual content. Pretrained VLMs degrade significantly on negated expressions Dobreva and Keller (2021) ; Singh et al. (2024) . NeIn Bui et al. (2025) shows that image-editing models struggle to remove or exclude specified content under negative instructions, while NegBench Alhamoud et al. (2025) finds that modern VLMs struggle to distinguish retained from excluded content in negated retrieval and reasoning. Thus, visual negation requires both semantic understanding and correct grounding of exclusion relations. VLAs such as OpenVLA Kim et al. (2025) , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} Intelligence et al. (2025) , and GR00T N series Bjorck et al. (2025) map language-conditioned visual observations to robot actions. Recent work has begun to address negative and corrective language: Hi Robot Shi et al. (2025) handles negative feedback through hierarchical reasoning, PGPS Kim et al. (2026) reduces forbidden-region grasp violations through inference-time steering, and LILAC Cui et al. (2023) enables online language correction in shared autonomy. However, these methods depend on hierarchical reasoning, external grounding, or online interaction. How negated semantics alter visual grounding within an end-to-end VLA and propagate to action generation remains underexplored.

sections.heading: 2.2 Language Conditioning and Instruction Following in VLAs
sections.text: Natural language serves as a primary mechanism for task specification and generalization in VLAs Yao et al. (2023) . Nevertheless, task success alone does not establish effective linguistic grounding Dong et al. (2026) : VLAs may exploit visual shortcuts Zhao et al. (2026) , lose linguistic competence during downstream fine-tuning Zhang and Bisk (2026) , or execute visually plausible actions under semantically contradictory instructions Zhang et al. (2026) . Reliable instruction following in VLAs therefore requires the policy to remain sensitive to linguistic semantics, rather than being dominated by visual cues and degenerating into a language-agnostic imitation policy. Effective language grounding must ultimately propagate from linguistic semantics through visual representations to action generation. Recent work strengthens this coupling by using language and execution history to reweight task-relevant visual tokens Xiao et al. (2026) . Motivated by this requirement, we propose NegaAlign, a parameter-efficient, plug-and-play framework for following negated instructions without costly negation-specific robot demonstrations.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: Figure 2: Overview of the purposed NegaAlign framework: (a) shows the construction of only vision and language data, (b) Negation Transformation Layer revises intermediate instruction representations, while (c) Teacher-Guided Visual Alignment transfers the revision of language representations to instruction-relevant visual tokens. As shown in Figure 2 , we present our NegaAlign framework for understanding negation, enabling reliable instruction following. We first define the problem in Section 3.1 and introduce how to construct negation supervision from existing affirmative demonstrations in Section 3.2 , then we introduce the Negation Transformation Layer for transferring semantic information of instructions in Section 3.3 and the Teacher-Guided Visual Alignment for aligning visual representations with negated instructions in Section 3.4 . Finally, we present the training recipe to make the VLAs adapt to the negated instructions efficiently in Section 3.5 .

sections.heading: 3.2 Negation Supervision Construction
sections.text: Existing embodied demonstrations encode individual skills with affirmative instructions in different fine-grained levels, telling robots what to do, such as pick up the hamburger or place the fries on the plate . However, people will specify what not to do in daily life, such as place any food except the chips on the plate . Considering the cost of collecting negation-specific robot demonstrations, we construct negation supervision from existing affirmative demonstrations and hand-crafted negated instructions. Specifically, we expose the latent structure of negation constraint as relational supervision, associating each negated instruction with a set of admissible affirmative interpretations and an explicitly excluded one, as illustrated in Figure 2 (a). The former defines where the negated semantics should be routed, while the latter provides the contrast needed to identify what should be suppressed. We formalize this relation as ℛ = ( ℓ n , 𝒜 , ℓ e ) \mathcal{R}=\left(\ell^{n},\,\mathcal{A},\,\ell^{e}\right) , where ℓ n \ell^{n} is a negated instruction, 𝒜 = { ℓ 1 a , … , ℓ M a } \mathcal{A}=\left\{\ell_{1}^{a},\ldots,\ell_{M}^{a}\right\} is the set of affirmative instructions satisfying its constraint, and ℓ e \ell^{e} describes the excluded behavior. For example, given place any foo d except the chips on the plate , the instructions for the hamburger and fries belong to 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , while the chips instruction is ℓ e \ell^{e} . During the stage of negation adaption, we first sample a tuple, then one satisfying instruction ℓ a ∈ 𝒜 \ell^{a}\in\mathcal{A} , and finally an observation–state pair ( 𝐨 , 𝐬 ) (\mathbf{o},\mathbf{s}) from its affirmative trajectory. The student branches use f θ , ϕ f_{\theta,\phi} , whereas the teacher branches use the same frozen f θ f_{\theta} without NTLs. Their outputs are denoted by 𝒪 S a \mathcal{O}_{S}^{a} , 𝒪 S n \mathcal{O}_{S}^{n} , 𝒪 T a \mathcal{O}_{T}^{a} , and 𝒪 T e \mathcal{O}_{T}^{e} . Sharing the observation and state across branches isolates the language contrast and turns existing affirmative data into negation supervision.

sections.heading: 3.4 Teacher-Guided Visual Alignment
sections.text: Related work on negation understanding of VLMs Kang et al. (2026) focus on how to enhance the negation semantics in the language space, however, VLAs not only need to understand the negation semantics, but also need to attend to the visual representations that are used for action generation. Therefore, revising the language representations alone by Negation Transformation Layers (NTLs) is insufficient to reliably alter the generated actions and the language representation revision should also be propagated to the instruction-relevant visual tokens. To achieve this goal, we purpose Teacher-Guided Visual Alignment (TGVA), which guides the revised negation semantics from the language space into the visual representations used for action generation. sections.heading: 3.5 Training Recipe
sections.text: Nowadays, the usual training recipe of VLAs is to first pretrain with large-scale embodied demonstration data, then fine-tune it on the task- or scenario-specific demonstration data for adaptation and generalization. Accordingly, NegaAlign follows a two-stage training recipe after the initial pretraining. Stage 1 fine-tunes the pretrained VLA on affirmative robot demonstrations, which is consistent with the standard fine-tuning process. Then during Stage 2, the fine-tuned VLA is frozen, Negation Transformation Layers (NTLs) are inserted, and they are trained with Teacher-Guided Visual Alignment (TGVA) using vision-language data constructed from the existing affirmative demonstrations. This stage requires neither negated action trajectories nor additional robot demonstrations. The training objective of Stage 2 is defined as follows: ℒ total = 1 | Ω | ​ ∑ l ∈ Ω ( ℒ equiv l + ℒ sem l + α ​ ℒ gate l ) , \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}=\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\sum_{l\in\Omega}\left(\mathcal{L}^{l}_{\mathrm{equiv}}+\mathcal{L}^{l}_{\mathrm{sem}}+\alpha\mathcal{L}^{l}_{\mathrm{gate}}\right), (9) where Ω \Omega is the set of layers with NTLs, and α \alpha is a hyperparameter to balance the three objectives. The objective is optimized to revise the intermediate instruction representations of negated instructions and propagate the negation semantics to the instruction-relevant visual tokens, thereby enabling the VLA to understand negation semantics and follow negated instructions. sections.heading: 3.6 Negation Instruction Following Benchmark Construction
sections.text: To systematically evaluate whether robots can follow negated constraints during manipulation, we construct NegaBench, a controlled and fine-grained benchmark built upon the RoboTwin simulation environment Chen et al. (2026a) . NegaBench comprises 10 manipulation scenarios spanning five representative categories of negation: object exclusion, attribute exclusion, relative comparison, goal-location exclusion, and combinations of multiple constraints. These categories progress from selecting among individual objects to executing complex behaviors that must satisfy several exclusions simultaneously. Each scenario provides semantically paired affirmative and negated instructions together with explicit constraint-aware success criteria: an execution is considered successful only if the robot completes the shared manipulation goal without violating any excluded object, attribute, or outcome specified by the instruction. By evaluating paired instructions under the same scene, manipulation skills, and success conditions, NegaBench controls for basic task competence and scene difficulty, directly measures whether a negated constraint changes the behavioral choice of robot, and systematically exposes the limitations of existing VLA models in constraint-aware instruction following. Complete benchmark construction and instruction relations are provided in Appendix B , and the evaluation protocol is detailed in Appendix C.1 .

sections.heading: 4.2 Comparison Results on NegaBench
sections.text: As shown in Table 1 , affirmative-only training yields strong affirmative performance but generalizes poorly to negated instructions: GR00T, π 0 \pi_{0} , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} achieve average negated success rates of 1.05%, 15.40%, and 2.60%, respectively. Explicit negated-trajectory training raises these rates to 68.85%, 71.25%, and 88.60%. This contrast motivates NegaAlign to ground negated constraints in existing manipulation skills rather than relearn the skills themselves. APT reaches 75.46% affirmative success but only 8.20% negated success with affirmative-only training, indicating that preserving the capabilities of VLM in a VLA is insufficient to solve the negated instruction follow problem. Qwen- π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} directly rewrites negated instructions into affirmative commands, yet achieves only 55.70% negated success and 71.58% affirmative success. This approach adds an upstream VLM inference step at every action-chunk request, increasing inference latency and making the action depend on the VLM visual grounding and instruction rewrite capabilities. Its substantially lower negated success than 88.45% of our purposed NegaAlign suggests that direct instruction rewriting is not an effective solution to negated instruction following in this setting. Without using any negated action trajectories, NegaAlign reaches 57.75%, 63.30%, and 88.45% negated success on GR00T, π 0 \pi_{0} , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , gains of 56.70, 47.90, and 85.85 percentage points over their corresponding Pos. baselines. Affirmative success is 72.89%, 68.41%, and 92.51%, respectively, compared with 71.09%, 68.20%, and 92.77% for Pos. FT . Averaged across the three models, it achieves 69.83% negated success, reaching 91.6% of the performance obtained through direct negated-trajectory training. On π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , NegaAlign achieves 88.45%, nearly matching the 88.60% of Pos.& Neg. These results demonstrate that semantic supervision constructed from existing affirmative data enables effective negated instruction following without additional robot demonstrations.

sections.heading: How do language semantics influence action generation?
sections.text: We first examine how language information affects the action generator. Figure 5 in left reports the action separation between satisfying and excluded instructions under two attention masks, normalized by the separation under full attention, where 1 1 indicates full preservation. When action queries cannot attend to text keys, the separation remains near 1 in deeper layers, showing that direct language access has little effect on the final actions. In contrast, blocking image queries from text keys causes the separation to approach zero, leaving the policy unable to distinguish the two instructions at the action level. Language semantics therefore primarily condition visual representations, which subsequently guide the action expert to generate actions. This observation of visual mediation motivates the design of Teacher-Guide Visual Alignment (TGVA).

sections.heading: Why is Teacher-Guide Visual Alignment(TGVA) effective?
sections.text: Based on the above analysis, we visualize the layer-wise differences of visual tokens between satisfying and excluded instructions in Figure 5 right. The visual differences between instructions are negligible in shallow layers, emerge and concentrate on instruction-relevant objects in middle layers, and spread toward background and irrelevant regions in deeper layers. Therefore, TGVA is designed to align the negated branch with the satisfying teacher in middle layers, where semantic visual grounding has formed but has not yet become diffuse. Removing TGVA reduces negated success from 88.45% to 21.35%, while affirmative success remains relatively high at 91.27%, as Table 2 shows. It indicates that NTL could preserve the original manipulation capability but cannot reliably propagate the revised semantics into action generation without TGVA, confirming the necessity of visual alignment and the effectiveness of the visual mediation mechanism identified in Figure 5 left.

sections.heading: What is the optimal intervention depth for Negation Transformation Layers(NTL)?
sections.text: As shown in Table 2 , inserting NTLs into middle layers of the VLM backbone yields the best performance in both affirmative and negated instruction following. Meanwhile, moving NTL to shallow or deep layers reduces negated success to 85.10% and 62.20%, respectively, while affirmative performance remains close to 92%. It indicates that the instruction-dependent visual representations have different characteristics in different layers, and the middle layers provide the best intervention point for NTLs, after semantic grounding emerges but before it becomes diffuse, which is consistent with the analysis in Figure 5 right.

sections.heading: Why is the NTL design necessary?
sections.text: As shown in Table 2 , retaining TGVA while removing NTL yields 86.65% negated success but collapses affirmative performance from 92.51% to 40.52%. In this variant, the proposed NTL is replaced by a trainable ungated revision layer at the same insertion positions, while all pretrained VLA parameters remain frozen. The replacement applies revision to both affirmative and negated instructions and is optimized using the semantic alignment and TGVA objectives. The decrease in performance highlights the importance of NTL in maintaining the performance of affirmative instructions. Specifically, visual alignment can induce constraint-satisfying behavior, but without controlled semantic transformation it also disrupts affirmative instructions. NTL separates semantic content from polarity and gates revision only when needed, enabling the complete model to achieve 88.45% negated success while retaining 92.51% affirmative success. Thus, NTL prevents this revision from compromising the original capabilities of policy while TGVA propagates revised semantics through action-relevant visual tokens.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We present NegaAlign, a parameter-efficient framework that combines Negation Transformation Layers and Teacher-Guided Visual Alignment to enable negated instruction following in pretrained VLAs without additional negated action trajectories. We also introduce NegaBench to evaluate this capability in robotic manipulation. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in negated instruction following while preserving affirmative performance. The limitations of this work include the reliance on existing pretrained VLAs, which may not cover all possible negated scenarios, and the potential for performance degradation in highly complex or ambiguous negated instructions that leads our direction of future work.

sections.heading: A.1 Backbones, Trainable Modules, and Branch Execution
sections.text: We instantiate NegaAlign from an affirmative-only checkpoint of each VLA. During negation post-training, all parameters inherited from the checkpoint are frozen, including the visual encoder, the vision–language backbone, the action expert or action head, and any adapters learned during affirmative training. The only trainable parameters are the inserted Negation Transformation Layers (NTLs). For π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , we insert NTLs before VLM layers 6–13 (one-based indexing). For GR00T, whose vision–language interface contains four Vision–Language Self–Attention (VLSA) blocks, we insert NTLs before the first three blocks and use the following block to obtain the Key and Value supervision signal. These configurations introduce 11.6M trainable parameters for π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and 4.35M for GR00T. The additional APT baseline uses its affirmative-trained checkpoint and executes dual-arm end-effector pose and gripper actions. Qwen- π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} pairs the affirmative-trained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} checkpoint with an unmodified Qwen3-VL-2B-Instruct model. At each action-chunk request, Qwen receives the current top-camera image and original instruction and generates a command for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ; both affirmative and negated instructions pass through this rewriting step. Each pair is expanded into four logical language-conditioned branches over the same observation and robot state: the affirmative student S a S^{a} , negated student S n S^{n} , satisfying teacher T a T^{a} , and excluded teacher T e T^{e} . Consequently, a training step with B = 4 B=4 evaluates 16 branch instances, but this should not be interpreted as either four model replicas or an optimization batch size of 16. All branches share one set of VLA weights. The two teachers are stateless, no-gradient forward branches of the same frozen checkpoint with the NTLs bypassed; they are neither separately trained networks nor exponential-moving-average copies. The number of independent scenes contributing to the stochastic gradient remains four. For π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , the two student branches are concatenated and executed as one gradient-carrying batch of size 2 ​ B 2B . The satisfying and excluded teachers are then evaluated as two sequential no-gradient batches of size B B . Thus, when B = 4 B=4 , the largest forward that retains activations for backpropagation contains eight samples, while each teacher forward contains four. Frozen image encoding and prompt embedding are also evaluated without constructing an autograd graph. This scheduling provides the four required representations without storing the activations of all 4 ​ B 4B branches simultaneously. GR00T further reuses computation across branches. Its frozen Qwen backbone jointly processes the satisfying, negated, and excluded language variants as a batch of size 3 ​ B 3B ; the satisfying hidden states are shared by T a T^{a} and S a S^{a} . The subsequent VLSA computation consists of two no-gradient teacher branches of size B B and one gradient-carrying student branch of size 2 ​ B 2B . Images are preprocessed once per sampled scene and repeated only after preprocessing. Hence, with B = 4 B=4 , Qwen receives 12 language variants, while the downstream VLSA blocks realize the same 16 logical branch instances required by the objective. Post-training executes only the visual–language prefix and the selected VLM blocks required to construct the intermediate supervision. It does not execute the action expert and does not consume action targets. This substantially reduces memory relative to running four complete VLAs, although compute still scales with the teacher and student branch forwards described above. At inference time, all teacher branches are discarded. The input instruction is revised by the learned NTLs at the same insertion sites, after which the frozen action-generation procedure of the original VLA is executed unchanged.

sections.heading: A.3 Teacher-Guided Visual Alignment
sections.text: TGVA uses two frozen forward branches to determine both where negation changes visual grounding and which affirmative grounding the negated student should approach. For every sampled scene, the satisfying teacher 𝒪 T a \mathcal{O}_{T}^{a} receives the selected admissible affirmative instruction and the excluded teacher 𝒪 T e \mathcal{O}_{T}^{e} receives the prohibited affirmative instruction. They share exactly the same image and robot state. Both branches bypass all NTLs and run without gradients, ensuring that their difference is caused only by the language condition rather than scene variation or teacher adaptation. An NTL is applied immediately before selected layer l l . We execute that layer and observe the visual keys and values projected at the input of layer l + 1 l+1 ; hence the observer measures the first visual representation that has incorporated the revised language through a complete attention block. For π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , image tokens form equal contiguous camera blocks, and we use the first, top-camera block. For GR00T, we use the 88 tokens identified by the processor as the coordinate-consistent cam_high block. Keys are measured after positional rotation and values after their value projection. The fourth GR00T VLSA block is not revised and serves only as the observer for the NTL before block 3. For a candidate visual token i i , we average cosine distance over KV heads and over keys and values: D i l ​ ( A , B ) = 1 2 ​ H kv ​ ∑ h = 1 H kv [ 1 − cos ⁡ ( 𝐤 A , i , h l , 𝐤 B , i , h l ) + 1 − cos ⁡ ( 𝐯 A , i , h l , 𝐯 B , i , h l ) ] . We select the token indices Φ b l = { i ∣ d b , i l > μ b l + s b l } , Ψ b l = { Φ b l , | Φ b l | ≥ k , TopK k ( d b , : l ) , | Φ b l | < k , \Phi_{b}^{l}=\{i\mid d_{b,i}^{l}>\mu_{b}^{l}+s_{b}^{l}\},\qquad\Psi_{b}^{l}=\begin{cases}\Phi_{b}^{l},&|\Phi_{b}^{l}|\geq k,\\ \operatorname{TopK}_{k}(d_{b,:}^{l}),&|\Phi_{b}^{l}|<k,\end{cases} (14) where TopK k \operatorname{TopK}_{k} returns the indices of the k k largest scores. sections.heading: B.1 Simulation Data Collection and Composition
sections.text: We construct the simulation data in RoboTwin 2.0 using SAPIEN and the dual-arm ALOHA-AgileX embodiment. The benchmark contains two scenes for each of five negation categories—object, attribute, comparison, goal, and complex—giving 10 scenarios in total. Across their affirmative and negated semantic variants, the environment defines 38 language-conditioned tasks. Objects, attributes, relative relations, and target placements are varied through seeded scene initialization. Demonstrations are generated by the task-specific scripted expert using motion-planned grasping and placement primitives. A trajectory is retained only when motion planning succeeds and the binary success predicate of task is met. Each retained episode stores the seed, instruction, joint trajectory, end-effector state, and synchronized RGB observations. The raw HDF5 files contain four 320 × 240 320\times 240 camera streams (front, head, left wrist, and right wrist) and a 14-dimensional action vector ordered as the six left-arm joints, left gripper, six right-arm joints, and right gripper. The models use the head and two wrist views after conversion to the common LeRobot format. The collected training corpus contains 2,360 episodes and 402,241 frames at 30 FPS. It comprises 38 task groups: 25 affirmative groups with 1,560 episodes and 13 explicitly negated groups with 800 episodes. Groups contain either 40 or 80 successful episodes. The explicit negated trajectories are used only by the fully supervised Pos.+Neg. baseline. Stage 1 affirmative training and NegaAlign Stage 2 do not use their observations, states, or actions. sections.heading: B.2 Real-World Data Composition
sections.text: The real-world dataset is collected on a UFACTORY xArm6 and contains 500 affirmative demonstrations, totaling 208,070 frames (approximately 1.93 hours) at 30 FPS. It covers 10 tasks with 50 episodes per task. The tasks form five semantic contrast pairs: spoon versus knife, separated versus mixed food, shirt versus socks, leaving versus storing a diamond, and ceramic versus stainless-steel bowls. No negated robot demonstration is included in this dataset. The data follow the LeRobot v2.1 organization, with one Parquet trajectory and two synchronized MP4 streams per episode. The overhead camera is recorded at 1920 × 1080 1920\times 1080 and the wrist-mounted tool camera at 640 × 480 640\times 480 . Each frame contains a 7-dimensional state and action vector ordered as 3-D position, 3-D rotation, and gripper position. The 10 tasks are balanced by episode count, although their durations differ: the dataset has a mean of 416.14 frames per episode, with lengths ranging from 229 to 1,027 frames. For Stage 1, all 500 affirmative episodes are available to train the base policy. sections.heading: B.4 End-to-End Post-Training Pipeline
sections.text: The Stage 2 loader first samples a relation uniformly, then samples a satisfying instruction uniformly from its set, and finally samples a frame uniformly from all episodes associated with that instruction. This hierarchical procedure prevents relations with more satisfying alternatives, longer trajectories, or more frames from dominating the objective. Simulation observations are repacked as the three ALOHA policy views and a 14-dimensional state; real-world observations are repacked as overhead/tool views and a 7-dimensional state. We apply the same input transforms and quantile normalization used by the corresponding Stage 1 policy, resize images to 224 × 224 224\times 224 , tokenize the prompt, and explicitly mark only the instruction-token span. Actions may be read by the common dataset interface, but they are never supplied as a Stage 2 target and do not contribute to any NegaAlign loss. For every sampled ( 𝐨 , 𝐬 , ℓ a ) (\mathbf{o},\mathbf{s},\ell^{a}) , the pipeline retrieves its relation and re-tokenizes the same observation–state pair with ℓ n \ell^{n} and ℓ e \ell^{e} . It constructs a joint 2 ​ B 2B student batch containing ( ℓ a , ℓ n ) (\ell^{a},\ell^{n}) and two B B -sized, no-gradient teacher branches containing ( ℓ a , ℓ e ) (\ell^{a},\ell^{e}) . The affirmative and negated student samples receive polarity targets 0 and 1, respectively. The satisfying teacher provides the semantic and visual destination, whereas the difference between satisfying and excluded teachers selects the TGVA visual tokens. The three losses in Eq. 9 update only the NTL parameters. The teacher branches and all original VLA components remain frozen, and the action expert is not executed during post-training. Architecture and optimizer details are provided in Appendix A . At inference time, relation lookup and both teacher branches are removed. A single observation, state, and user instruction pass through the frozen VLA augmented with the trained NTLs, after which the original action generator produces the action chunk. Thus, the additional training structure has no teacher-model cost at deployment.

sections.heading: C.1 NegaBench Evaluation Protocol
sections.text: All simulation policies are evaluated through the same RoboTwin client–server pipeline. The client owns environment initialization, instruction selection, rollout, success checking, and result logging, while a model-specific server only converts observations to an action chunk. This separation permits each VLA to use its own software environment without changing the benchmark logic. For every evaluated task variant, we run 100 episodes. Candidate initialization seeds are first executed by the scripted expert of task; a seed is admitted only when motion planning succeeds and the expert satisfies the same task-specific success predicate used for policy evaluation. The resulting task/config-specific seed list is cached and reused across policies. We fix the task manifest, task configuration, seed group, checkpoint, normalization statistics, and action execution horizon for each comparison. At each closed-loop step, the policy receives the instruction, a head-view image, two wrist-view images, and its model-specific proprioceptive state. The π 0 \pi_{0} , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and GR00T adapters execute 14-dimensional dual-arm joint-position actions. APT instead executes 16-dimensional dual-arm end-effector pose and gripper actions. A predicted chunk is truncated to the minimum of the configured execution horizon (32), the returned chunk length, and the remaining episode budget. The environment checks success throughout low-level action execution and terminates on the first successful state or after 300 high-level actions. Each episode produces a binary outcome. For affirmative instructions, success requires completing the requested manipulation. For negated instructions, it additionally requires respecting every exclusion constraint. For task k k with N = 100 N=100 episodes, we report SR k = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N 𝕀 ⁡ [ episode ​ i ​ succeeds ] . \mathrm{SR}_{k}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{I}[\text{episode }i\text{ succeeds}]. (17) Category and overall values in the main paper are macro-averages of the corresponding task-level success rates, so tasks with longer trajectories do not receive additional weight. Corresponding author. Abstract Instruction following enables robots to perform diverse tasks specified in natural language, making it a fundamental capability for human–robot interaction. Beyond communicating desired outcomes, users also need to specify constraints on what not to do . We investigate how to enable vision-language-action models (VLAs) to follow negated instructions, where robots must accomplish task goals while respecting explicit exclusions. To this end, we propose NegaAlign, a parameter-efficient, plug-and-play framework that extends pretrained VLAs to follow negated instructions through image–language supervision alone. Specifically, we introduce Negation Transformation Layers into selected layers of the vision–language backbone to reshape intermediate instruction representations. Meanwhile, teacher-guided alignment mechanism is designed to align the instruction-relevant visual tokens, transferring action-relevant grounding from instructions that satisfy the negated constraint. Training phase uses supervision constructed from existing demonstrations and updates only the inserted layers, keeping all pretrained parameters frozen, including the action generator. We further introduce NegaBench, a simulation benchmark spanning 10 scenarios across five domains for systematically evaluating manipulation under negated constraints. Experiments across GR00T, π 0 \pi_{0} , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} demonstrate consistent improvements in negated instruction following. With 11.6M trainable parameters, NegaAlign increases the negated-instruction success rate of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} from 2.60% to 88.45% on NegaBench and from 12.4% to 88.8% on real-world tasks, while retaining performance on affirmative instructions. 1 Introduction Figure 1: Existing VLAs struggle with negated instructions, risking unsafe actions. Our proposed NegaAlign enables actions under negated constraints. As robots enter daily life, reliable instruction following is crucial for both human and robot safety. Vision Language Action models (VLAs) Zitkovich et al. (2023) ; Kim et al. (2025) ; Intelligence et al. (2025) ; Bjorck et al. (2025) follow natural language instructions and perform manipulation tasks in complex environments. Pretraining on large-scale embodied datasets O’Neill et al. (2024) enables them to complete a wide range of manipulation tasks, including pick-and-place, tool use, and object rearrangement. However, these existing VLAs are mostly trained on affirmative instructions and struggle to follow negated instructions. This limitation can result in unsafe or undesired actions Chen et al. (2026b) ; Lyu et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2025) , as the robot may act on the affirmative content of the instruction without considering the negated constraints. For example, given ”Give me a tool, except the knife”, a robot will still hand the knife to the user, which is an extremely dangerous behavior in daily life, as illustrated in Figure 1 (a). A key source of this problem lies in the VLMs backbone, whose difficulty in understanding negation affects the action sequence generation of VLAs further. Existing studies investigate negation understanding in image-text matching Dobreva and Keller (2021) ; Aggarwal et al. (2026) , image editing Bui et al. (2025) , and image-grounded object detection Kang et al. (2026) ; Yang et al. (2026) , which could not be applied to the VLAs directly since the VLAs need to ground the negated instruction into the sequence of actions to complete the task. Recent approaches improve VLA instruction following through hierarchical decomposition and fine-grained supervision Zawalski et al. (2024) ; Zhu et al. (2024) . Hi Robot Shi et al. (2025) uses an additional VLM to decompose instructions into subtasks, introducing extra inference computation. APT Xu et al. (2026) adopts two-stage pretraining to better preserve VLM knowledge in the action expert, but requires a dedicated multi-stage training procedure, while Fine-VLA Hu et al. (2026) constructs fine-grained instruction data to strengthen language-action alignment. However, collecting negation-specific robot demonstrations is costly and time-consuming. Hence, how to enable existing VLAs to follow negated instructions without additional negation-specific embodied data remains an unexplored problem. To address these challenges, we propose NegaAlign, a parameter-efficient, plug-and-play framework for following negated instructions without costly negation-specific embodied data for the reliable instruction following. Our key insight is that when action expert generates the action sequences, most information are provided by the visual tokens, while the vision tokens are grounded by the instruction text representations. Specifically, we firstly construct teacher-student instruction pairs from existing affirmative-task data and hand-crafted negated instructions without additional negation-specific action data. Subsequently, we propose sophisticated Negation Transformation Layers into selected layers of the VLM backbone to revise intermediate instruction representations of negated instructions, which help to modulate the instruction representations to be more compatible with the negated constraints. Meanwhile, we apply teacher-guided alignment to instruction-relevant visual tokens. The alignment propagates the revised instruction representations to the visual tokens which is beneficial for the action generation. Training phase updates only the inserted layers using image–language supervision, while the pretrained backbone and action expert remain frozen. To evaluate the capability of reliable instruction following, we establish NegaBench, a simulation benchmark spanning 10 scenarios across five domains for systematically evaluating manipulation under negated constraints. Experiments on the NegaBench and real-world robot demonstrate that NegaAlign significantly improves the success rate of negated instruction following across various scenarios with fewer update of parameters. The main contributions of this work are listed as follows: • We present the first investigation of negated instruction understanding and execution in VLAs, revealing how semantics from language instructions are encoded in internal representations and gradually propagate through the model to shape action generation. • We propose NegaAlign, a plug-and-play framework which revises instruction representations through Negation Transformation Layers and propagates negation semantics to visual representations through Teacher-Guided Visual Alignment, enabling VLAs to follow negated constraints efficiently by updating only a few number of parameters. • We establish NegaBench, a benchmark for systematically evaluating robotic manipulation under negated instructions. Experiments in simulation and real-world robot demonstrate that NegaAlign substantially improves negated instruction following across multiple existing VLAs while preserving performance on affirmative instructions. 2 Related Work 2.1 Negation in Language, Vision, and Action Negation remains challenging for large language models (LLMs) despite their strong general capabilities. Evaluations show that LLMs degrade on negated prompts, sometimes worsening with scale, and struggle with negated commonsense knowledge Jang et al. (2023) ; Wang et al. (2026) . Mechanistic analyses further reveal that shortcut behaviors can disrupt how LLMs suppress or reconstruct negated meanings Zhou et al. (2026) . Similar challenges arise in vision-language models (VLMs), where negated semantics must be grounded in visual content. Pretrained VLMs degrade significantly on negated expressions Dobreva and Keller (2021) ; Singh et al. (2024) . NeIn Bui et al. (2025) shows that image-editing models struggle to remove or exclude specified content under negative instructions, while NegBench Alhamoud et al. (2025) finds that modern VLMs struggle to distinguish retained from excluded content in negated retrieval and reasoning. Thus, visual negation requires both semantic understanding and correct grounding of exclusion relations. VLAs such as OpenVLA Kim et al. (2025) , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} Intelligence et al. (2025) , and GR00T N series Bjorck et al. (2025) map language-conditioned visual observations to robot actions. Recent work has begun to address negative and corrective language: Hi Robot Shi et al. (2025) handles negative feedback through hierarchical reasoning, PGPS Kim et al. (2026) reduces forbidden-region grasp violations through inference-time steering, and LILAC Cui et al. (2023) enables online language correction in shared autonomy. However, these methods depend on hierarchical reasoning, external grounding, or online interaction. How negated semantics alter visual grounding within an end-to-end VLA and propagate to action generation remains underexplored. 2.2 Language Conditioning and Instruction Following in VLAs Natural language serves as a primary mechanism for task specification and generalization in VLAs Yao et al. (2023) . Nevertheless, task success alone does not establish effective linguistic grounding Dong et al. (2026) : VLAs may exploit visual shortcuts Zhao et al. (2026) , lose linguistic competence during downstream fine-tuning Zhang and Bisk (2026) , or execute visually plausible actions under semantically contradictory instructions Zhang et al. (2026) . Reliable instruction following in VLAs therefore requires the policy to remain sensitive to linguistic semantics, rather than being dominated by visual cues and degenerating into a language-agnostic imitation policy. Effective language grounding must ultimately propagate from linguistic semantics through visual representations to action generation. Recent work strengthens this coupling by using language and execution history to reweight task-relevant visual tokens Xiao et al. (2026) . Motivated by this requirement, we propose NegaAlign, a parameter-efficient, plug-and-play framework for following negated instructions without costly negation-specific robot demonstrations. 3 Method Figure 2: Overview of the purposed NegaAlign framework: (a) shows the construction of only vision and language data, (b) Negation Transformation Layer revises intermediate instruction representations, while (c) Teacher-Guided Visual Alignment transfers the revision of language representations to instruction-relevant visual tokens. Finally, we present the training recipe to make the VLAs adapt to the negated instructions efficiently in Section 3.5 . 3.1 Problem Formulation We assume that a vision–language–action model (VLA) has been pretrained on large-scale robot demonstrations and has acquired the affirmative skills required by the target tasks. Accordingly, NegaAlign follows a two-stage training recipe after the initial pretraining. Stage 1 fine-tunes the pretrained VLA on affirmative robot demonstrations, which is consistent with the standard fine-tuning process. Then during Stage 2, the fine-tuned VLA is frozen, Negation Transformation Layers (NTLs) are inserted, and they are trained with Teacher-Guided Visual Alignment (TGVA) using vision-language data constructed from the existing affirmative demonstrations. This stage requires neither negated action trajectories nor additional robot demonstrations. (2026a) . NegaBench comprises 10 manipulation scenarios spanning five representative categories of negation: object exclusion, attribute exclusion, relative comparison, goal-location exclusion, and combinations of multiple constraints. These categories progress from selecting among individual objects to executing complex behaviors that must satisfy several exclusions simultaneously. Each scenario provides semantically paired affirmative and negated instructions together with explicit constraint-aware success criteria: an execution is considered successful only if the robot completes the shared manipulation goal without violating any excluded object, attribute, or outcome specified by the instruction. By evaluating paired instructions under the same scene, manipulation skills, and success conditions, NegaBench controls for basic task competence and scene difficulty, directly measures whether a negated constraint changes the behavioral choice of robot, and systematically exposes the limitations of existing VLA models in constraint-aware instruction following. We first examine how language information affects the action generator. Figure 5 in left reports the action separation between satisfying and excluded instructions under two attention masks, normalized by the separation under full attention, where 1 1 indicates full preservation. When action queries cannot attend to text keys, the separation remains near 1 in deeper layers, showing that direct language access has little effect on the final actions. In contrast, blocking image queries from text keys causes the separation to approach zero, leaving the policy unable to distinguish the two instructions at the action level. Language semantics therefore primarily condition visual representations, which subsequently guide the action expert to generate actions. This observation of visual mediation motivates the design of Teacher-Guide Visual Alignment (TGVA). Why is Teacher-Guide Visual Alignment(TGVA) effective? Based on the above analysis, we visualize the layer-wise differences of visual tokens between satisfying and excluded instructions in Figure 5 right. The visual differences between instructions are negligible in shallow layers, emerge and concentrate on instruction-relevant objects in middle layers, and spread toward background and irrelevant regions in deeper layers. Therefore, TGVA is designed to align the negated branch with the satisfying teacher in middle layers, where semantic visual grounding has formed but has not yet become diffuse. Removing TGVA reduces negated success from 88.45% to 21.35%, while affirmative success remains relatively high at 91.27%, as Table 2 shows. It indicates that NTL could preserve the original manipulation capability but cannot reliably propagate the revised semantics into action generation without TGVA, confirming the necessity of visual alignment and the effectiveness of the visual mediation mechanism identified in Figure 5 left. What is the optimal intervention depth for Negation Transformation Layers(NTL)? As shown in Table 2 , inserting NTLs into middle layers of the VLM backbone yields the best performance in both affirmative and negated instruction following. Meanwhile, moving NTL to shallow or deep layers reduces negated success to 85.10% and 62.20%, respectively, while affirmative performance remains close to 92%. It indicates that the instruction-dependent visual representations have different characteristics in different layers, and the middle layers provide the best intervention point for NTLs, after semantic grounding emerges but before it becomes diffuse, which is consistent with the analysis in Figure 5 right. Why is the NTL design necessary? As shown in Table 2 , retaining TGVA while removing NTL yields 86.65% negated success but collapses affirmative performance from 92.51% to 40.52%. In this variant, the proposed NTL is replaced by a trainable ungated revision layer at the same insertion positions, while all pretrained VLA parameters remain frozen. The replacement applies revision to both affirmative and negated instructions and is optimized using the semantic alignment and TGVA objectives. The decrease in performance highlights the importance of NTL in maintaining the performance of affirmative instructions. Specifically, visual alignment can induce constraint-satisfying behavior, but without controlled semantic transformation it also disrupts affirmative instructions. NTL separates semantic content from polarity and gates revision only when needed, enabling the complete model to achieve 88.45% negated success while retaining 92.51% affirmative success. We also introduce NegaBench to evaluate this capability in robotic manipulation. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate substantial improvements in negated instruction following while preserving affirmative performance. The limitations of this work include the reliance on existing pretrained VLAs, which may not cover all possible negated scenarios, and the potential for performance degradation in highly complex or ambiguous negated instructions that leads our direction of future work.
